beats.say: In the winter of twenty twenty one, a typical household energy bill in Britain was capped at around twelve hundred pounds a year. Within a year, households were paying around two and a half thousand, and that was with government help. Without it, the cap would have been far higher.

Here's how the price cap for a typical household moved. Around twelve hundred pounds in winter twenty twenty one to twenty two. Nearly nineteen hundred in spring twenty twenty two. Over three thousand three hundred that autumn. And over four thousand at the start of twenty twenty three.

vis.title: Ofgem price cap, typical household (per year)

beats.say: Part one. What is the price cap?

First, what's the price cap? It's set by the energy regulator, Ofgem. It limits how much suppliers can charge for each unit of energy, and the standing charge, on standard tariffs. It isn't a cap on your total bill. If you use more, you pay more.

vis.text: A cap on unit prices, not your total bill.

beats.say: The cap is based mainly on the wholesale cost of gas and electricity, plus network costs, policy costs and suppliers' operating costs. So when wholesale prices soar, the cap follows, a few months later.
The cap is updated every three months now. Before twenty twenty two, it changed only twice a year. Faster updates mean bills follow wholesale prices more closely, both up and down.
Part two. Why prices exploded.

Wholesale gas prices began rising in twenty twenty one, as economies reopened after the pandemic and demand jumped. A cold winter, low gas storage in Europe, and weak wind power added to the pressure.
Then, in February twenty twenty two, Russia invaded Ukraine. Russia had been one of Europe's biggest gas suppliers. Fears over supply sent gas prices to record highs.

vis.text: Then came the invasion of Ukraine.

beats.say: But Britain gets little of its gas directly from Russia. So why did bills soar here too? Because gas is traded on international markets. When European prices spike, British prices spike too.
And because gas power stations often set the price of electricity, electricity bills rose sharply too, even though much of Britain's electricity comes from other sources like wind and nuclear.

vis.text: Gas often sets the price of electricity.

beats.say: Britain relies heavily on gas, both for heating most homes through gas boilers, and for generating a large share of electricity. That made the country especially exposed to the gas price shock.
Part three. Suppliers collapsed.

Many small energy suppliers had sold fixed price deals without protecting themselves against rising wholesale costs. When prices soared, they couldn't cope. Dozens went bust in twenty twenty one and twenty twenty two.

One of the biggest, Bulb, with around one and a half million customers, was put into special administration and run by the government before being sold. The costs of supplier failures were added to everyone's bills.
Part four. Government help.

In October twenty twenty two, the government introduced the Energy Price Guarantee. It limited the typical household bill to around two thousand five hundred pounds a year, with the government paying suppliers the difference.
Households also received a four hundred pound energy bills support discount over the winter, and extra payments went to people on certain benefits, pensioners and disabled people.
The support cost the government tens of billions of pounds. Without it, many more households would have fallen into fuel poverty.
Businesses didn't have a price cap. Many saw energy bills multiply when their contracts renewed, which led some pubs, bakeries and factories to close or raise prices.

vis.text: Businesses had no cap at all.

beats.say: Part five. Where are we now?

Wholesale prices have fallen from their peak. But bills haven't gone back to where they were. From October twenty twenty six, the cap for a typical household was set at around one thousand seven hundred and twenty pounds a year, still well above the pre crisis level.

vis.title: Typical household cap
vis.source: Ofgem price cap, as reported Aug 2026

beats.say: Standing charges, the fixed daily cost you pay even if you use no energy, have also risen. And the costs of supplier failures, network upgrades and debt are spread across bills.
Ofgem has also introduced a requirement for suppliers to offer at least one tariff with a lower standing charge, for households who use little energy.

vis.text: Lower standing charge options for low users.

beats.say: Part six. What can you do?

You can't control the global gas market. But you can check whether a fixed tariff is cheaper than the cap, submit regular meter readings, improve insulation, and make sure you're getting any support you're entitled to.
Britain's energy shock showed how connected we are to world events. A war a thousand miles away changed what millions of families paid to heat their homes.

vis.text: A distant war changed every bill.
